To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) multiple microclimate gradients drive variation in demographic rates and population performance across a species range, 2) climate change can perturb population stability through size dependent responses of demographic rates, 3) species range shifts will be mediated by the differential and size dependent response of demographic transitions to changing climate, and 4) climate change will lead to a shift in alpine plant communities towards less diverse, warmer, drier adapted plant communities.

(1) the differential response of demographic transitions to experimental warming leads to a universal contraction of populations across the elevatinal range of I. lycopodioidesscandularis and (2) experimental warming results in a shift towards dominance of hot dry adapted species in alpine plant communities.

1) multiple microclimactic gradients shape demographic rates and range wide population growth of a focal species, 2) climate change will perturb this population growth and lead to range wide population contractions, 3) climate change will shift the alpine plant community towards dominance by warm, dry adapted species, and 4) the effects of climate change on population growth and community composition were not ameliorated or enhanced by experimental summertime additions of precipitation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the population and community dynamics of an alpine plant species in response to changing climate.
the population and community dynamics of alpine plants in a changing climate.
understanding the population and community dynamics of a montane plant species in the face of climate change across topographically heterogeneous terrain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of a changing climate on alpine plants are complex.
I found that multiple gradients shape population performance in a species across a heterogeneous landscape and that this leads to stable range wide populations.

topographically heterogeneous landscapes can decouple climate gradients, leading to a complex mosaic of climate conditions across a landscape that may drive species range shifts in a non linear fashion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the effects of climate change on species range dynamics are complexly influenced by multiple climate gradients, life history transitions, and community interactions, and that these interactions will shape the rate and magnitude by which plant populations and communities will shift in a changing climate. the effects of climate change on alpine plants are not straightforward.
species distributions are not simply shifting in response to a warming climate.

species range shifts will be mediated by the degree of variation in demographic performance across species ranges, and that the effects of changing climate will be most severe where species are most sensitive to climate.
